paper.title: Positive interactions promote public cooperation
paper.research_question: Whether positive targeted interactions can sustain cooperation in repeated public goods games as effectively as punishment and with higher payoffs.
paper.sample: 192 subjects at Harvard Business School Computer Lab for Experimental Research
paper.setting: Anonymous computer-mediated repeated groups of four with persistent group membership

game_context.baseline_condition: Standard repeated public goods game with no targeted second-stage interaction

mechanisms.name: Costly targeted reward after each public-goods round
mechanisms.summary: After observing group contributions, players can direct rewards to specific group members, enabling positive reciprocity toward contributors and maintaining high cooperation with higher total earnings than punishment-only settings.

actors.observer: Group members via repeated interaction and persistent identities

timing.stage: Second stage after each public-goods contribution round

information_structure.anonymity: Subjects anonymous but interacted with the same three people throughout; identities persisted within group
public_information: Prior round contributions available for targeted response
information_structure.history_visibility: Player identities persist across rounds, allowing behavior toward specific individuals to condition on past contributions

action_space_changes.range_or_options: For each other group member: reward or no action
action_space_changes.condition: Available in RN and RNP treatments after PGG stage

payoff_changes.amount_or_formula: Costly reward; exact cost-benefit ratio not specified in provided excerpt

state_variables.name: contribution_history_by_player
state_variables.update_rule: Record each player's PGG contribution each round for future targeted decisions

state_variables.name: reward_actions
state_variables.update_rule: Record directed reward choices between players after each round

state_variables.name: total_payoff
state_variables.update_rule: PGG payoff plus reward-stage costs and benefits

prompt_requirements: Tell agents they remain with the same group across rounds.
Show or summarize each group member's prior contribution before targeted reward choices.
Allow agent to choose reward/no action for each other group member.

metrics.name: average_contribution
metrics.definition: Mean amount contributed to the public pool per round

metrics.name: reward_frequency
metrics.definition: Fraction of possible directed reward actions used

metrics.name: average_total_payoff
metrics.definition: Mean payoff including PGG and targeted interaction payoffs

metrics.name: percent_maximum_possible_payoff
metrics.definition: Achieved payoff as a percentage of full-cooperation/full-reward benchmark

minimal_code_changes: Add post-PGG targeted reward stage with directed choices for each ordered pair.
Expose contribution history or last-round contributions to agents.
Apply reward costs and benefits to payoffs.
Log directed reward frequency and total payoff.
risks_or_assumptions: Exact reward cost-benefit parameters must be recovered from full methods or chosen as a calibrated assumption.
Persistent identities are essential; shuffling identifiers would change mechanism.

mechanisms.name: Costly targeted punishment after each public-goods round
mechanisms.summary: After observing contributions, players can punish specific group members, especially free riders, sustaining cooperation relative to no-targeted-interaction control but reducing payoffs through destructive costs.

actors.observer: Group members via persistent repeated interaction

timing.stage: Second stage after each public-goods contribution round

information_structure.anonymity: Anonymous to experimenters/real identities, but fixed in-game identifiers within group
public_information: Prior contributions available for targeted response
information_structure.history_visibility: Persistent identities allow direct reciprocity over rounds

action_space_changes.range_or_options: For each other group member: punish or no action
action_space_changes.condition: Available in PN and RNP treatments after PGG stage

payoff_changes.amount_or_formula: Costly punishment; exact cost and loss not specified in provided excerpt

state_variables.name: punishment_actions
state_variables.update_rule: Record directed punishment choices between players after each round

state_variables.name: punishment_frequency
state_variables.update_rule: Fraction of possible punishment actions used

prompt_requirements: Show agents each other member's contribution history or last contribution.
Allow punish/no-action choices toward each other group member.

metrics.name: punishment_frequency
metrics.definition: Fraction of possible directed punishment actions used

metrics.name: average_total_payoff
metrics.definition: Mean payoff net of punishment costs and target losses

minimal_code_changes: Apply punisher cost and target loss.
Log punishment use and net payoff.
risks_or_assumptions: Punishment may be antisocial or retaliatory, not only directed at free riders.
Exact sanction parameters need full methods.

mechanisms.name: Combined reward, no-action, and punishment targeted interaction
mechanisms.summary: Players can choose reward, no action, or punishment toward each other after each PGG round. When both positive and negative reciprocity are available, reward use increases contributions and payoffs, while punishment does not improve contributions and lowers payoff.

timing.stage: Second stage after each PGG round

information_structure.history_visibility: Same partners throughout session, enabling direct reciprocity

action_space_changes.range_or_options: reward, no action, punishment for each other group member

payoff_changes.who_receives_or_loses: Reward target gains; punishment target loses
payoff_changes.amount_or_formula: Costly directed interaction; exact amounts not in provided excerpt

state_variables.name: targeted_interaction_matrix
state_variables.update_rule: For every ordered player pair, store reward/no-action/punishment each round

state_variables.name: net_targeted_payoff
state_variables.update_rule: Accumulate costs paid and benefits/losses received from targeted interactions

prompt_requirements: For each other player, ask agent to choose reward, no action, or punishment after seeing contribution information.

metrics.name: reward_vs_punishment_frequency
metrics.definition: Relative use of reward and punishment over time

metrics.name: contribution_by_treatment
metrics.definition: Mean contribution under control, PN, RN, and RNP

metrics.name: payoff_by_treatment
metrics.definition: Mean total payoff under control, PN, RN, and RNP

minimal_code_changes: Add configurable targeted-interaction treatment with option set {reward, none, punish}.
Maintain stable player IDs and per-player histories.
Compute directed interaction payoffs and log use over time.
risks_or_assumptions: Reward and punishment effects are not additive.
Requires simultaneous or well-defined directed choices among all ordered pairs.

requires_baseline_extension: Treatment flags for control, PN, RN, RNP
implementation_order: Add persistent player IDs and contribution history
Expose history and action options in prompts
Add metrics for contributions, reward/punishment frequency, and total payoff

experiment_design.baseline_condition: Repeated PGG only, no targeted interactions
treatment_conditions: PN: punishment or no action after each PGG round
RN: reward or no action after each PGG round
RNP: reward, no action, or punishment after each PGG round
control_variables: subjects not told total number of rounds

cooperation_outcomes: Reward-only and reward-plus-punishment were equally effective in maintaining cooperation.
Reward treatments generated larger absolute payoffs than punishment-only.
evidence.reported_effect_direction: Targeted interactions increase cooperation versus control; reward matches punishment for cooperation and outperforms punishment on total earnings.
key_quotes_or_passages: Reward is as effective as punishment for maintaining public cooperation and leads to higher total earnings.
When both options are available, reward leads to increased contributions and payoff, while punishment has no effect on contributions and leads to lower payoff.
It is not punishment per se which is important for sustaining contributions, but rather the possibility of targeted interactions.

uncertainties: Exact number of rounds and exact reward/punishment cost-benefit parameters are not available in the provided excerpt.
